# wfmR

`wfmR` contains Will Mackey's R chart defaults and Quarto formats for research
notes, policy briefs, papers, and slides.

```{r colours}
wfm_colours()
```

## Palette and Tints

```{r colour-demo, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.4}
tint_strengths <- c(100, 80, 60, 40)
palette_names <- names(wfm_palette())
palette_tints <- map_dfr(
  palette_names,
  function(colour) {
    base <- wfm_palette()[colour]
    values <- c(
      base,
      wfm_tints(base, strength = tint_strengths[-1])
    )
    names(values) <- paste0(
      colour,
      ifelse(tint_strengths == 100, "", tint_strengths)
    )

    data.frame(
      colour = tools::toTitleCase(colour),
      variant = factor(names(values), levels = names(values)),
      strength = factor(tint_strengths, levels = tint_strengths),
      hex = unname(values),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  }
)
palette_tints$colour <- factor(
  palette_tints$colour,
  levels = tools::toTitleCase(palette_names)
)

ggplot(palette_tints, aes(colour, 1, fill = hex, group = strength)) +
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.9),
    width = 0.22
  ) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  labs(
    title = "Primary colours and selected tints",
    subtitle = "Each group shows the base colour, then 80, 60, and 40 percent strengths",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_wfm(grid = FALSE) +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )
```

```{r tints}
wfm_tints(wfm_colours("teal", "salmon", "yellow", "pink"), strength = c(90, 60, 30, 10))
```

The default colours are also available as objects:

```{r colour-objects}
c(
  wfm_salmon,
  wfm_teal,
  wfm_purple,
  wfm_lime,
  wfm_yellow,
  wfm_blue,
  wfm_pink
)
```

Tint constants use the percentage of original colour retained: `wfm_teal90`
is close to teal, while `wfm_teal10` is very pale.

```{r tint-objects}
c(wfm_teal90, wfm_teal70, wfm_teal50, wfm_teal30, wfm_teal10)
```

The primary palette is checked under severe deutan, protan, and tritan
simulation. The full seven-colour palette is shown because it is the default
brand/chart sequence; for dense categorical encodings, use direct labels or
additional aesthetics when colours may be hard to distinguish.

```{r colour-blind-report}
wfm_colour_blind_report()
```

Available discrete, sequential, and diverging options:

```{r palette-options}
wfm_palette_options()[, c("type", "name", "generator", "notes")]
```

## Categorical Palettes

Discrete chart scales use `scale_fill_wfm()` or `scale_colour_wfm()`. The
primary palette is the package default; the Wong/Colour Universal Design palette
is retained as a colour-blind-friendly backup via `palette = "colourblind"` or
`palette = "wong"`.

```{r categorical-data, include=FALSE}
primary_values <- c(31, 27, 24, 21, 18, 16, 13)
publication_values <- c(31, 27, 24, 21, 18, 16, 13, 10)

primary_df <- tibble(
  group = factor(str_to_title(names(wfm_palette())), levels = str_to_title(names(wfm_palette()))),
  value = primary_values
)

wong_df <- tibble(
  group = factor(
    str_to_title(names(wfm_palette(palette = "colourblind"))),
    levels = str_to_title(names(wfm_palette(palette = "colourblind")))
  ),
  value = publication_values
)

mtcars_cyl <- mtcars |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "car") |>
  mutate(cyl = factor(cyl))
```

### Primary

```{r categorical-primary-chart}
primary_df |>
  ggplot(aes(group, value, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  scale_fill_wfm(palette = "primary") +
  scale_y_wfm(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(
    title = "Primary categorical palette",
    subtitle = "The default wfmR order: salmon, teal, purple, lime, yellow, blue, pink",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Value",
    caption = "Illustrative data."
  ) +
  theme_wfm()
```

### Publication Backup

```{r categorical-wong-chart}
wong_df |>
  ggplot(aes(group, value, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72) +
  scale_fill_wfm(palette = "colourblind") +
  scale_y_wfm(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(
    title = "Colour-blind-friendly categorical palette",
    subtitle = "The original Colour Universal Design palette remains available",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Value",
    caption = "Illustrative data."
  ) +
  theme_wfm()
```

### Categorical Scatter

```{r categorical-scatter-chart}
mtcars_cyl |>
  ggplot(aes(wt, mpg, colour = cyl)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, alpha = 0.88) +
  scale_colour_wfm(palette = "primary") +
  scale_y_wfm() +
  labs(
    title = "Categorical colour also works for points",
    subtitle = "Cylinder count is mapped to the primary palette",
    x = "Weight (1,000 lbs)",
    y = "Miles per gallon",
    caption = "Source: R datasets package."
  ) +
  theme_wfm()
```

## Sequential Palettes

Sequential palettes are for ordered quantities. Each facet below uses one
available sequential palette.

```{r sequential-data, include=FALSE}
volcano_df <- as_tibble(as.data.frame(as.table(volcano))) |>
  transmute(
    x = as.integer(Var1),
    y = as.integer(Var2),
    height = Freq,
    signal = height - mean(height)
  ) |>
  filter(x %% 2 == 1, y %% 2 == 1)

seq_names <- wfm_palette_options("sequential") |>
  filter(type == "sequential") |>
  pull(name)

seq_labels <- str_to_title(str_replace_all(seq_names, "_", " "))

seq_df <- map_dfr(seq_names, function(palette) {
  ramp <- wfm_sequential_palette(palette, n = 256)
  index <- pmax(1, pmin(256, round(scales::rescale(volcano_df$height, to = c(1, 256)))))

  volcano_df |>
    mutate(
      palette = palette,
      palette_label = str_to_title(str_replace_all(palette, "_", " ")),
      fill = ramp[index]
    )
}) |>
  mutate(palette_label = factor(palette_label, levels = seq_labels))
```

```{r sequential-palettes-chart, fig.height=7}
seq_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, fill = fill)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  coord_equal(expand = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(vars(palette_label), ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Sequential palette options",
    subtitle = "Each panel maps the same ordered surface using one wfmR sequential palette",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: R datasets package."
  ) +
  theme_wfm(grid = FALSE) +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

## Diverging Palettes

Diverging palettes are for quantities centred on a meaningful midpoint. Each
facet below maps the same centred surface around zero.

```{r diverging-data, include=FALSE}
div_names <- wfm_palette_options("diverging") |>
  filter(type == "diverging") |>
  pull(name)

div_labels <- str_to_title(str_replace_all(div_names, "_", " "))

div_df <- map_dfr(div_names, function(palette) {
  ramp <- wfm_diverging_palette(palette, n = 257)
  index <- pmax(
    1,
    pmin(257, round(scales::rescale_mid(volcano_df$signal, to = c(1, 257), mid = 0)))
  )

  volcano_df |>
    mutate(
      palette = palette,
      palette_label = str_to_title(str_replace_all(palette, "_", " ")),
      fill = ramp[index]
    )
}) |>
  mutate(palette_label = factor(palette_label, levels = div_labels))
```

```{r diverging-palettes-chart, fig.height=7}
div_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x, y, fill = fill)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  coord_equal(expand = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(vars(palette_label), ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Diverging palette options",
    subtitle = "Each panel maps the same zero-centred surface using one wfmR diverging palette",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: R datasets package."
  ) +
  theme_wfm(grid = FALSE) +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

## Quarto

Create a new Quarto document and install the bundled extension beside it:

```{r quarto-usage, eval=FALSE}
library(wfmR)

use_wfmr_doc("analysis.qmd", format = "html")
use_wfmr_doc("serif-analysis.qmd", format = "html", serif = TRUE)
use_wfmr_doc("paper.qmd", format = "pdf")
use_wfmr_doc("working-paper.qmd", format = "all", style = "academic", serif = TRUE)
use_wfmr_doc("slides.qmd", format = "revealjs")
```

For an existing document, install the extension once with:

```{r quarto-extension, eval=FALSE}
use_wfmr_extension()
```

The default `"nice"` style uses `wfmr-html` for HTML notes and `wfmr-pdf` for
LaTeX/PDF documents. It gives charts a Grattan-style heading above the figure,
with subtitles also above and notes/sources below. The `"academic"` style uses
`wfmr-academic-html` and `wfmr-academic-pdf`; it gives academic PDFs a title
page with an abstract, places figure captions below figures, places table
captions above tables, and keeps subtitles, notes, and sources with the same
float. Slides use `wfmr-revealjs`.

The extension supplies the chart-notes Lua filter, chart cross-reference
defaults, HTML/revealjs theme files, and LaTeX header file automatically. The
YAML below shows the main document options you can override directly. Standard
Quarto options can be added in the same place.

### Style Notes

- The primary chart palette now follows a softer Rose Pine-inspired direction:
  salmon, teal, purple, lime, yellow, blue, and pink. Green remains available
  as an exported constant, but is excluded from the primary chart order because
  it sits too close to lime in this palette. The Wong/Colour
  Universal Design palette is retained as `palette = "colourblind"` or
  `palette = "wong"`.
- The HTML and revealjs formats include a Quarto `_brand.yml` layer with light
  Dawn and dark Moon colour mappings, after the base Bootswatch theme and before
  the package SCSS. LaTeX/PDF uses the same palette in `latex-header.tex`
  because Quarto brand files do not currently style LaTeX output.
- Tints are generated by mixing each primary colour towards white. For example,
  `wfm_teal90` keeps 90 percent of teal and `wfm_teal10` is close to white.
- Sequential and diverging scales are derived from the primary colours and
  their tints, using OKLab interpolation for smoother continuous gradients.
- The nice HTML format follows `topics/course-notes.qmd` and the eyes writeups:
  Quarto `cosmo`/`darkly`, embedded resources, code annotations/folding/tools,
  optional left table of contents, SVG plots, chart headings above figures, and
  notes/sources below figures.
- HTML documents can opt into serif prose by setting `mainfont`, or by calling
  `use_wfmr_doc(..., serif = TRUE)`. The serif option bundles Newsreader as a
  local variable WOFF2 font, with Georgia, Cambria, Iowan Old Style, and
  Palatino fallbacks. Charts, code, navigation, and table of contents UI stay
  in the system sans-serif stack. The bundled Newsreader files are included
  under the SIL Open Font License in `inst/quarto/_extensions/wfmr/fonts/newsreader/`.
- The generic coloured labels, note block, and chart notes come from
  `R/styles.css`, `case-study/eyes/code/chart-labels.R`, and
  `case-study/eyes/code/chart-notes.lua`.
- The nice PDF format comes from `case-study/eyes/writeup-nontechnical.qmd`: A4
  `article`, 11pt type, 1.2 line stretch, black citation/link colour, chart
  captions, and a LaTeX header adapted from Pascal Michaillat's paper template
  using Source Serif Pro when available, centred bold section headings, bold
  subsections, italic run-in paragraph headings, and French spacing.
- The academic HTML/PDF formats keep the same page, palette, and chart defaults,
  opt into serif prose for HTML, and use bottom captions and quieter figure notes
  for papers, working papers, and thesis chapters.
- The revealjs theme is derived from the HTML rules: system UI type, restrained
  headings, Rose Pine links, the same chart metadata, and the same package
  palette.

### Nice Article YAML: HTML + PDF

``` yaml
---
title: "Research note"
subtitle: "One page of text and one chart"
author: "Will Mackey"
brand: "_extensions/wfmr/_brand.yml"
format:
  wfmr-html:
    fig-format: svg
    embed-resources: true
    code-annotations: below
    code-fold: show
    code-tools: true
    toc: true
    toc-location: left
    toc-depth: 3
    toc-expand: true
    fig-cap-location: top
    df-print: paged
  wfmr-pdf:
    documentclass: article
    papersize: a4
    geometry:
      - top=1in
      - left=1.3in
      - right=1.3in
      - bottom=1.2in
      - footskip=0.7in
    fontsize: 11pt
    linestretch: 1.2
    toc: false
    colorlinks: true
    linkcolor: black
    citecolor: black
    urlcolor: black
    link-citations: true
    link-bibliography: true
    fig-cap-location: top
    tbl-cap-location: top
    fig-pos: tb
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
crossref:
  fig-title: Chart
  fig-prefix: Chart
---
```

### Academic Article YAML: HTML + PDF

``` yaml
---
title: "Working paper"
subtitle: "Formal figure captions"
author: "Will Mackey"
brand: "_extensions/wfmr-academic/_brand.yml"
abstract: |
  A short abstract or overview sits on the title page below the author block.
  The academic PDF format clears the page after the abstract before starting the
  body text.
format:
  wfmr-academic-html:
    fig-format: svg
    mainfont: "Newsreader, Georgia, Cambria, Iowan Old Style, Palatino Linotype, Palatino, serif"
    linestretch: 1.58
    embed-resources: true
    code-annotations: below
    code-fold: show
    code-tools: true
    toc: true
    toc-location: left
    toc-depth: 3
    toc-expand: true
    fig-cap-location: bottom
    df-print: paged
  wfmr-academic-pdf:
    documentclass: article
    papersize: a4
    geometry:
      - top=1in
      - left=1.3in
      - right=1.3in
      - bottom=1.2in
      - footskip=0.7in
    fontsize: 11pt
    linestretch: 1.2
    toc: false
    colorlinks: true
    linkcolor: black
    citecolor: black
    urlcolor: black
    link-citations: true
    link-bibliography: true
    fig-cap-location: bottom
    tbl-cap-location: top
    fig-pos: tb
    include-in-header:
      text: |
        \wfmAcademicAuthor{Will Mackey}{Australian National University}{Author note for the title-page footnote.}
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
crossref:
  fig-title: Chart
  fig-prefix: Chart
---
```

### revealjs YAML

``` yaml
---
title: "Presentation"
author: "Will Mackey"
brand: "_extensions/wfmr/_brand.yml"
format:
  wfmr-revealjs:
    embed-resources: true
    fig-format: svg
    slide-number: c/t
    show-slide-number: all
    preview-links: auto
    transition: fade
    background-transition: fade
    controls: true
    progress: true
    smaller: false
    code-line-numbers: false
    footer: ""
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
crossref:
  fig-title: Chart
  fig-prefix: Chart
---
```

[Source QMD](examples/wfmr-revealjs-demo.qmd) |
[revealjs example](examples/wfmr-revealjs-demo.html)

revealjs screenshot:

![](man/figures/wfmr-demo-revealjs.png)

In a setup chunk, call:

```{r chart-defaults, eval=FALSE}
library(wfmR)
wfm_chart_defaults()
wfm_chart_defaults(style = "academic")
```

Plot chunks can then use `chart-title`, `chart-subtitle`, `chart-notes`, and
`chart-source` chunk options. In nice documents, the title/subtitle render as
above-chart headings. In academic PDFs, chart titles render as plain formal
captions below figures, table titles render above tables, and the subtitle,
notes, and source render in a smaller block with the same float. The bundled
Lua filter renders notes and sources in HTML, PDF, and revealjs outputs.
